title: Alamosa East Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Alamosa East wells have a 110 ft median depth, but records range to 3,080 ft. See yield, water levels, costs and local risks.
h1: Alamosa East Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land in Alamosa East means looking beyond whether a parcel has a well permit. The local records show shallow typical wells, strong reported yields, and a very wide range of drilling depths. Among permitted wells within five miles, the median depth is 110 feet, while the middle half runs from 40 to 400 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 3,080 feet.

These figures are a starting point for a site-specific investigation, not a guarantee. Only 247 wells report a pump yield and 99 report a static water level, so neighboring records are useful but incomplete. Check the permit, well construction report, water right, and intended use before closing or starting construction.

sections.heading: Alamosa East well depth depends on the ground below
sections.html:
Depth varies substantially around Alamosa East. Forty-five percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, and 24% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 10% are 300 to 600 feet, while 20% are deeper than 600 feet. The median is 110 feet, but the 90th percentile is 850 feet.

For a drilling bid, that spread matters more than the median alone. A nearby shallow well may be a useful comparison, but it does not rule out a deeper hole on your lot. The records name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers for 1,279 wells, along with the Confined San Luis Valley aquifer for 356 and the Unconfined San Luis Valley aquifer for 280. Mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground can still change from parcel to parcel.

sections.heading: Reported well yields are generally strong, with limited testing
sections.html:
The reported yield data are favorable, but the sample is small compared with the total record. Only 247 wells report a pump yield. Among those, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty-nine percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 39% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

One percent report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and none are recorded under 1 gallon per minute. That does not mean every new well will produce 15 gallons per minute. Ask for the well test and permitted use. A household well also has legal limits and may need an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin, especially if the proposed use goes beyond the permit.

sections.heading: Water levels are shallow, but the decade comparison deserves a check
sections.html:
The median static water level is 7 feet below land surface, with the middle half from 0 to 12 feet. That is shallow water compared with the range of drilling depths, and it can affect casing, grout, excavation, and septic planning. A shallow water table also means surface activities deserve careful attention.

The decade summary shows a median static level of 0 feet below surface in the 2010s and 9 feet below surface in the 2020s. That is a deeper recent median in this record, but only 99 wells report static water levels, and measurements may be taken at different locations and conditions. Treat it as a signal to investigate, not proof of a basin-wide decline. Have a driller or hydrogeologist review nearby measurements for your parcel.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long local drilling experience
sections.html:
Alamosa East has a long permit record. The Colorado Division of Water Resources records show 31 permits from the 1950s, 45 from the 1960s, 442 from the 1970s, 162 from the 1980s, 425 from the 1990s, 339 from the 2000s, 262 from the 2010s, and 137 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in the data is 2025.

The most active drillers in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 167 wells; Rocky Mountain Waterworks LLC (Phythian, Donald L.), with 122; and Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.), with 83. Those names identify local permit history, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, insurance, references, and who will perform the test, casing, grout, pump installation, and final paperwork.

sections.heading: A median-depth well pencils out differently from a deep one
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground reported here, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $75 per foot. At the 110-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $5,500 to $8,200. That is only the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $11,500 to $20,200 at the median depth. A bid for a parcel with a nearby 600-foot or deeper comparison should not be based on the median alone. Ask how the estimate handles extra casing, difficult material, grouting, pump setting depth, power service, access, and a dry or low-yield result. Get the permit and intended-use requirements priced separately.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic separation, and the chance of a bad hole
sections.html:
Environmental screening around Alamosa East finds 10 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are no historic mine features mapped in that radius. These findings do not establish contamination at your parcel, but they are enough reason to test the well for the substances relevant to the property and its surroundings.

Low yield is not the only risk. A well can be deep, poorly constructed, or unsuitable for the intended household, stock, or irrigation use. Keep the well, septic system, leach area, and replacement area laid out together before building. Confirm access for a rig, electrical service, casing and grout details, water quality, and the permit's allowed use. In Alamosa, Mosca, La Jara, Sanford, Blanca, and Monte Vista, conditions can differ from the immediate Alamosa East records.

sections.heading: Use nearby records before buying or laying out a new home
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not a countywide assumption. Pull the DWR permit and construction report, then compare neighboring wells by depth, aquifer description, yield, static level, and date. Alamosa is about 2 miles away, while Mosca, La Jara, Sanford, Blanca, and Monte Vista are farther reference areas; the closest comparable wells should carry the most weight.

For a purchase, make water rights, well inspection, flow testing, and laboratory testing part of the contract and due diligence period. For a new build, confirm the well can serve the planned fixtures and that septic setbacks work with the actual water level and lot geometry. Have a Colorado-licensed driller review access and probable depth before relying on the $11,500 to $20,200 finished-system estimate.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Alamosa East?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth near Alamosa East is 110 feet. The middle half ranges from 40 to 400 feet, but the area also has wells deeper than 600 feet, with a 90th-percentile depth of 850 feet and a deepest recorded depth of 3,080 feet. A nearby well is useful evidence, not a guarantee for a new hole.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Alamosa East?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 110-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $5,500 to $8,200. A finished system including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $11,500 to $20,200. Greater depth, difficult ground, access, and electrical requirements can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Alamosa East?
faq.a: Among the 247 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty-nine percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. Because most records do not include a yield, require a test on the specific well and verify the permitted use.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Alamosa East?
faq.a: The records do not prove drinking-water safety. There are 10 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, so testing is important. Have the well sampled by a qualified laboratory and review construction, casing, grout, septic location, and nearby land uses before relying on it for household water.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Alamosa East?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 0 feet below surface in the 2010s and 9 feet below surface in the 2020s. That is a deeper recent median, but only 99 wells report static levels, and measurements may not be comparable. The data suggest checking the trend, not claiming a basin-wide decline. Review nearby measurements with a qualified professional.
